extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of art history and modern/contemporary art
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the stylistic, technical, thematic and ideological characteristics and practices associated with the Surrealist movement in visual art and related media. Covers techniques, exhibition practices, sources of inspiration, and political/ideological aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of depictive, abstract and psychological
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristics of this style—a combination of the depictive, the abstract, and the psychological—came to stand for the alienation which many people felt in the modern period, combined with the sense of reaching more deeply into the psyche, to be "made whole with one's individuality".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should blend recognisable (depictive) imagery with abstraction and psychological/dream elements to evoke alienation and deeper psychic states. Example references: Magritte, Tanguy. No explicit scoring guidance; central definitional characteristic of Surrealist style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of liquid/melting forms (Dalí's motif)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquid shapes became the trademark of Dalí, particularly in his The Persistence of Memory, which features the image of watches that sag as if they were melting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing fluid, melting, or morphing forms as a visual motif to unsettle ordinary perception; used as a signature device by Dalí as illustration of dream logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial automatic techniques (fumage, coulage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paalen contributed Fumage and Onslow Ford Coulage as new pictorial automatic techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods that foreground automatism and chance in the making process (smoke impressions, pouring media, etc.). These techniques are cited as innovations within Surrealist pictorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assemblage, collage and found objects/photography
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism reached beyond painting, to encompass photography as well, as can be seen from a Man Ray self-portrait, whose use of assemblage influenced Robert Rauschenberg's collage boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate assemblage, collage, and found photographic elements into works; embrace appropriation and recombination of existing materials and images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition-as-creative-act / immersive installation design
rubrics_metrics.description: The Surrealists wanted to create an exhibition which in itself would be a creative act (example: the 1938 Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme with Rainy Taxi, Surrealist Street, a cave-like main hall of suspended coal bags, humid leaves and mud, aroma of roasting coffee, and patrons carrying flashlights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exhibitions as immersive, performative experiences that manipulate setting, scent, sound, lighting and audience action to produce disorientation or scandal. Example anti-pattern: conventional neutral white-cube presentation that avoids sensory or performative provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of the unconscious and dream imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas concerning the unconscious and dream imagery were quickly embraced by artists; dream imagery and unconscious processes are central Surrealist themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize imagery and procedures that reference dreams, the unconscious, and pschoanalytic themes. This principle undergirds many other techniques (automatism, juxtaposition, chance operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebration of spontaneity / instantaneous human act
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism (and its influence on Abstract Expressionism) celebrated the instantaneous human act as the well-spring of creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and foreground spontaneous gestures, improvisation and immediate production as sources of artistic authority; connect method to authenticity of psyche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition of disparate elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Magritte's work maintained the element of juxtaposition (unexpected combinations). The broader movement frequently uses startling juxtapositions of details and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create surprising, often dissonant combinations of objects, figures or motifs to generate new meanings. Important caveat (from quoted commentary): 'any old combination of details will not do'—juxtapositions should be managed with care and skill to avoid mere novelty or bad taste (Pynchon's/Spike Jones Jr. metaphor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chance operations and cut-up technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The cut-up technique, in which chance is used to dictate the composition of a text from words cut out of other sources, was developed with former surrealist Brion Gysin and used by William S. Burroughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ procedures that introduce randomness or aleatory ordering into composition (cut-ups, chance assemblage) to disrupt intentional authorship and reveal unexpected associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing on non-Western cultures for inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealists believe that non-Western cultures also provide a continued source of inspiration because some may induce a better balance between instrumental reason and imagination in flight than Western culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek influences beyond the Western canon as a deliberate strategy to rebalance reason and imagination; ethically contextualize and engage with non-Western sources rather than appropriating without understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political engagement: linking imagination to liberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealism has had an identifiable impact on radical and revolutionary politics, emphasizing the intimate link between freeing imagination and the mind, and liberation from repressive and archaic social structures (visible in New Left, May 1968 etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art can and often should be explicitly political: use surrealist methods to critique social structures and advance emancipatory aims. Consider historical precedents of Surrealists allying with radical movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application across media (theatre, dance, music, film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrealist techniques influenced theatre ('Theatre of the Absurd'), performance (Farley's elaborate costuming and improvisation), music (cut-up technique influence), and film (e.g., Jan Švankmajer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate Surrealist principles—automatism, juxtaposition, chance, shock—into other media while attending to medium-specific practices (costume, movement, sound design, montage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'found' images and catalog/presentation design
rubrics_metrics.description: Duchamp's design for an exhibition catalog included 'found', rather than posed, photographs of the artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ found photography and documentary fragments in presentation materials and catalogs to subvert conventional portraiture and authorship; use archival/found imagery strategically in exhibit narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biomorphic and organic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some artists (e.g., Yves Tanguy; Mark Rothko took an interest in biomorphic figures) explored biomorphic figures and organic shapes as part of Surrealist vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate organic, amoeboid or biomorphic shapes to suggest subconscious morphologies and to contrast with hard-edged realist elements.
